title: The Problem: Origin Distance and Roundtrip Latency
text: Hi, I'm Akshay. Open a website and its images, JavaScript, fonts, and video can appear almost instantly, even when the origin server is thousands of miles away. Sending every request all the way to that origin would add network distance and load. A content delivery network changes that path by placing content at edge locations around the world. So, what actually happens between your browser and that nearby edge? Start without a CDN. A user requests an asset from an origin on the other side of the

title: Distributed POPs and Smart Edge Routing
text: Country or even the world. The request crosses multiple networks before reaching the server, and the response has to travel back. Even when the origin is fast, physical distance and network hops add round-trip latency. Repeat that path for many assets and many users, and the delay becomes noticeable. A content delivery network adds distributed points of presence, or POPs, between users and the origin. Each POP contains edge infrastructure that can serve cached

title: Cache Hits: Serving Content Directly from the Edge
text: Content. Instead of every user depending on one distant origin, requests can be handled from edge infrastructure much closer in network terms to where the traffic enters the CDN. When the browser requests a CDN-hosted asset, the CDN's routing system directs that request toward an appropriate edge location. Providers can use DNS, anycast, health information, network topology, and current conditions to make that decision. The goal is not simply the

title: Cache Misses: Fetching and Reusing Upstream Objects
text: Geographically closest machine. It is to reach a healthy edge that can serve the request efficiently. From the application side, the URL can still look ordinary. The page references an asset on the CDN host name, and the browser makes an HTTPS request. The CDN accepts that request at its edge and checks whether the requested object is already cached there. That cache lookup determines whether the origin needs to be involved. On a cache hit, the edge

title: Caching Policies: Cache-Control, TTL, and Invalidation
text: Already has a fresh copy of the object. It can return the image, stylesheet, script, or video segment directly to the user. The request does not need to travel back to the origin for that object. That shorter path is one of the biggest reasons repeated content delivery can feel so fast. On a cache miss, the edge does not have a usable copy. Maybe this is the first request in that location or the cached object expired. The edge forwards the request

title: Summary: Why CDNs Make Global Content Feel Fast
text: Toward the origin or another configured upstream and waits for the response. This request pays more of the long-distance cost, but it can prepare the edge for later requests. The origin returns the object to the CDN edge. The edge forwards the response to the user and if the caching rules allow it, stores a copy locally. The first request may therefore be slower than a cache hit, but it turns the edge into a reusable delivery point for later users requesting the same content. Caching behavior is controlled by policy. For example, an origin can send cache control headers that tell shared caches whether an object is cacheable and how long it can remain fresh. A CDN can also apply its own configured rules. The important idea is that content is cached deliberately with freshness and invalidation behavior defined by

Policy. Now a second user near that edge requests the same object while it is still fresh. This time the edge can answer from its cache. The origin does no work for that request and the response travels over a shorter network path. Multiply that by popular assets in many edge locations and origin traffic can drop dramatically. Cached content cannot stay forever without a freshness strategy. A time to live can make an object expire after a configured period. Revalidation can ask whether an older copy changed while purge or invalidation mechanisms can remove content sooner when necessary. Longer caching improves reuse, but applications also need a plan for updates and stale content. CDNs are especially effective for reusable assets, images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, downloads, and video segments. Popular objects can be cached across many edge locations, so users in

Different regions do not all pull the same bytes from one origin. The CDN absorbs much of that repeated delivery work while the origin remains the authoritative source. So the speed comes from several mechanisms working together. Shorter network paths to edge infrastructure, cache hits that avoid origin round trips, and a distributed network built to deliver content at scale. But, not every request is cacheable. Misses, personalized responses, freshness requirements, and origin performance still matter. A CDN reduces expensive long-distance work. It does not eliminate the origin. The mental model is simple. Route the user to an appropriate edge, serve fresh cached content there when possible, fetch from the origin when necessary, and reuse that response for later requests. By moving repeated delivery closer to users and distributing it across many edge locations, CDNs make global content feel much faster.
